meta.subtitle: Aerospace and defense prime; Q2'26 sales $24.7B up 14%, backlog $289B up 22%, full-year guidance raised

analystCommentary: RTX enters the second half of 2026 with double-digit top-line growth and a raised full-year outlook. Q2'26 sales were $24.7B, up 14% versus the prior year and up 16% organically, with GAAP EPS of $1.57 and adjusted EPS of $1.89, {+ up 21% +}. Backlog stood at $289B, {+ up 22% +} year over year, split $170B commercial and $119B defense. Management raised its full-year adjusted EPS range to $7.10-$7.25 and free cash flow to $8.50-$8.75B. The shares trade at 34.0x trailing earnings and 26.7x forward (NTM), a premium that leaves limited room for execution slips. We rate RTX BUY with a $205-$255 target range against the $193.12 price, reflecting backlog-backed growth balanced against a rich multiple, the Pratt & Whitney Powder Metal Matter, and tariff and policy uncertainty.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: RTX Corporation is an aerospace and defense company serving commercial, military, and government customers worldwide. It operates through three segments: Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney, and Raytheon. Collins Aerospace supplies aerospace and defense products and aftermarket services, including power, environmental, flight-control, and cabin systems for civil and military aircraft. Pratt & Whitney supplies aircraft engines for commercial, military, business-jet, and general-aviation customers, along with auxiliary power units and aftermarket maintenance, repair, and overhaul services. Raytheon provides threat detection, tracking, and mitigation capabilities, including sensors and mission systems, for government and commercial customers. Raytheon follows a fiscal calendar, while Collins and Pratt & Whitney use calendar quarter ends. The company was formerly known as Raytheon Technologies Corporation and changed its name to RTX Corporation in July 2023. RTX was incorporated in 1934 and is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, with more than 180,000 employees and 2025 sales of more than $88 billion.

thesis.body: RTX pairs a large installed base of engines and aircraft systems with a defense franchise geared to rising munitions and missile-defense demand. Q2'26 sales grew 14% to $24.7B with wider segment margins, and backlog reached $289B, up 22% year over year. The aftermarket-heavy commercial mix and multi-year defense programs give revenue visibility, and management raised full-year adjusted sales, adjusted EPS, and free cash flow guidance. The counter-case is valuation: at 34.0x trailing and 26.7x forward earnings, the shares already discount continued execution, and the Powder Metal Matter, tariffs, and supply-chain constraints can each pressure margins or cash. Our BUY rests on backlog conversion outrunning these drags, not on further multiple expansion.

catalysts: Backlog conversion: the commercial and defense backlog, split $170B and $119B, underpins the raised full-year sales and EPS outlook as programs ship.
Defense funding: the proposed $1.5 trillion FY2027 defense budget and the July 2025 Act's $24.4B Golden Dome and $25.4B munitions provisions point to demand for RTX missiles and munitions.
Margin expansion across all three segments: Q2'26 return on sales improved at Collins, Pratt & Whitney, and Raytheon, with Pratt & Whitney reported ROS at 8.3%.
Portfolio actions: the agreed $620 million sale of Raytheon's Blue Canyon Technologies business sharpens the defense portfolio.
Tariff refunds: the roughly $0.5 billion of IEEPA tariffs paid since inception could be partly refunded following the CIT's refund order, subject to the government's June 2026 appeal.
risks: Rich valuation: the premium trailing and forward earnings multiples leave little margin for execution slips.
Powder Metal Matter: Pratt & Whitney's 2023 finding on powder metal in PW1100 GTF engines requires accelerated fleet inspection of A320neo aircraft.
Capital-return policy: an executive order may limit distributions and share repurchases during periods of defense-contractor underperformance.
Tariffs and supply chain: RTX faces IEEPA tariff costs pending refund and expects supply-chain disruptions to continue.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue rose from $64.4B in FY21 to $88.6B in FY25, a 9.7% increase in the latest year. Operating margin widened from 8.0% in FY21 to 10.5% in FY25, after a trough of 5.2% in FY23. FY25 operating income was $9.3B, net income $6.7B, and diluted EPS $4.96. The vendor's financial feed reports FY25 revenue as a single consolidated line, while the filing and the Q2'26 press release break the business into three operating segments, which we use for the segment detail. Momentum continued in Q2'26: revenue was $24.7B, up 14% by the press release's rounding, which the vendor's latest-quarter data shows as 14.5% — the same Q2'26 revenue-growth figure at a source and rounding difference. The Q2'26 operating margin was 11%, which the vendor's latest-quarter feed rounds to 11.4%; the report uses the 11% figure. On a trailing-twelve-month basis the operating margin was 11.2%. GAAP EPS was $1.57, up 29%, and adjusted EPS was $1.89, {+ up 21% +}, with net income attributable to common shareowners of $2,139 million and adjusted net income of $2,579 million, {+ up 22% +}. The FY23 margin trough shows the earnings sensitivity to charges and mix, so the recent margin recovery is the metric to watch.
financials.balanceCommentary: RTX ended FY25 with $8.2B of cash and short-term investments, $67.1B of total equity, and a current ratio of 1.03. The reported debt series is discontinuous: total debt runs $41.3B in FY24 to $0.2B in FY25, and net debt is shown at -$7.2B in FY25, a swing that reads as a data-source artifact rather than deleveraging of that scale. The proxy statement offers a grounded reference point, disclosing $3.4 billion of debt paydown during 2025. Given the discontinuity, we lean on the equity base, the near-1.0 current ratio, and disclosed capital-return capacity rather than the reported net-debt figure. The trailing-twelve-month current ratio is 1.01. On the evidence available, liquidity looks adequate, but the debt figure should be re-verified against the filing's balance sheet before it is used in any leverage calculation.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation improved in FY25: operating cash flow was $10.6B, capital expenditure -$2.6B, and free cash flow $7.9B, a 9.0% free-cash-flow margin and the strongest of the five-year series. Q2'26 free cash flow was {+ $2.9B +}, up from {- -$72 million -} a year earlier, on operating cash flow of $3.5B against $458 million and capital expenditure of $0.7B. Management raised the full-year free-cash-flow outlook to $8.50-$8.75B. FY25 dividends paid were -$3.6B and share repurchases -$0.1B, so the payout tilts to dividends. The trailing free-cash-flow yield is 4.4%. The swing from a negative prior-year quarter flatters the year-over-year comparison, so the full-year guide is the better gauge of run-rate cash generation.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: RTX trades at 34.0x trailing earnings, 2.8x sales, and 16.9x EV/EBITDA. On forward estimates the multiple steps down to 26.7x next-twelve-month earnings and about 24.6x FY27 earnings, consistent with consensus FY26E EPS of $7.24 and FY27E EPS of $7.85. The vendor supplies no peer multiples, so this is an absolute rather than a relative read. The Street consensus target is $234.41, a 21.4% premium to the current price, with a median of $240.00 and a range of $200.00 to $265.00; the rating split is 15 Buy, 8 Hold, 0 Sell. The premium trailing multiple sets a high bar, but the step-down on forward earnings reflects the double-digit growth already in the guide.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Backlog converts faster than planned and defense funding accelerates: sales track the upper end of the raised $95.0-$96.0B outlook, adjusted EPS reaches the top of $7.10-$7.25, munitions and missile-defense awards build on the $289B backlog, and the forward multiple holds near current levels.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: RTX executes to the raised full-year guide, backlog conversion sustains 8-9% organic growth, and the shares compound with earnings rather than through multiple expansion.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Multiple compression meets execution drag: the Powder Metal Matter, tariffs, and supply-chain constraints pressure margins, capital-return limits weigh on sentiment, and the rich 34.0x trailing multiple de-rates toward the lower half of the 52-week range near $155.64.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 50%, the Bull at 28%, and the Bear at 22%. That yields a probability-weighted fair value near $216, an expected upside of roughly 12% against the $193.12 price, and a bear-case downside of about 17%, for reward/risk near 0.7. Those inputs support a BUY under the desk's rule. Our $205-$255 target range brackets the $218 Base case; the Base sits below consensus, while the upper end of the range runs above the consensus target. The Bear case at $160 is a real scenario: it sits well below the current price and within the 52-week range, reflecting the Powder Metal Matter, tariff and policy uncertainty, and the risk that a premium multiple de-rates. The call depends on backlog conversion, not on the multiple expanding from here.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: RTX reports as a single consolidated line in the vendor feed but runs three operating businesses. Q2'26 consolidated sales were $24.7B, up 14%, and each business posted higher margins. Collins Aerospace sales were $8,210 million, up 8%, at a 15.9% return on sales. Pratt & Whitney sales were $8,889 million, up 16%, at an 8.3% return on sales. Raytheon sales were $8,269 million, up 18%, at a 12.6% return on sales, on higher volume across air and missile defense programs. The businesses span commercial aftermarket, aerospace original-equipment, and defense end markets.

moatFactors.name: Aftermarket installed base
moatFactors.body: Collins and Pratt & Whitney serve customers under long-term aftermarket service agreements covering spare parts and services. Q2'26 commercial aftermarket rose 10% at Collins and 25% at Pratt & Whitney, a recurring high-margin revenue stream tied to a large installed fleet that competitors cannot easily displace.

moatFactors.name: Defense incumbency and backlog
moatFactors.body: RTX is a prime contractor or subcontractor on a broad portfolio of defense programs, with $119B of defense backlog. Multi-year missile and munitions programs such as Patriot, Standard Missile, and AMRAAM provide visibility and high switching costs for government customers.

moatFactors.name: Certification and technology barriers
moatFactors.body: Aircraft engines and defense systems require extensive certification, qualification, and proven performance, which raises barriers to entry. The same demands cut both ways: untested technologies and fixed-price development contracts carry cost-overrun and performance risk.

moatFactors.name: Scale and diversification
moatFactors.body: With more than 180,000 employees and 2025 sales of more than $88 billion across three segments and commercial and defense end markets, RTX has scale and end-market diversification that soften single-program shocks.

businessMoat.durability: The moat rests on a large installed base of engines and aircraft systems that generate long-term aftermarket revenue, and on defense incumbency backed by the multi-year backlog cited above. These sources are durable: aftermarket agreements span years, and defense programs run multi-year with high switching costs. The main threats to durability are execution and policy, not competitive displacement. The Powder Metal Matter shows how a quality issue can impose accelerated inspections and cost, fixed-price development contracts can produce cost overruns, and an executive order could limit capital return during periods of contractor underperformance. Supply-chain disruptions and tariffs add cost pressure the company cannot always pass through on fixed-price contracts. On balance, the franchise is wide, but its returns depend on disciplined program execution.

points: Backlog conversion is the growth engine: the commercial and defense backlog ships over multi-year aftermarket and program cycles, turning today's order coverage into revenue and underpinning the raised organic-growth guide.
Management lifted FY2026 adjusted sales guidance to $95.0-$96.0B and organic growth to 8-9%, up from 5-6%, and adjusted EPS to $7.10-$7.25.
Consensus estimates put FY26E revenue at $96.1B and FY27E revenue at $103.2B, with EPS rising from $7.24 to $7.85.

Defense funding reaches RTX through munitions replenishment and next-generation missile-defense work: the Golden Dome initiative and munitions provisions map to RTX's missile and munitions franchises, with awards, timing, and appropriations the swing factors.
Q2'26 organic sales grew 16%, led by double-digit commercial aftermarket and defense volume, which shows demand converting ahead of the raised guide.

management.leadership: RTX is led by Chairman and CEO Chris Calio, who framed Q2'26 as double-digit organic growth with wider margins. Neil G. Mitchill, Jr. is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, with 11 years at RTX. The Raytheon segment is led by President Philip J. Jasper and Pratt & Whitney by President Shane G. Eddy. Management's stated priorities are executing the backlog, increasing productivity, expanding capacity, and introducing new technologies. The proxy notes the CFO oversaw financial performance that exceeded the adjusted sales, adjusted EPS, and free-cash-flow expectations communicated to investors for 2025, despite tariff and supplier headwinds.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation tilts to reinvestment and dividends. In 2025 RTX invested $7.7 billion in company- and customer-funded research and development and capital expenditures, increased its annual dividend rate by 7.9%, and returned over $3.6 billion of capital to shareowners, while paying down $3.4 billion of debt. The quarterly dividend rose from $0.63 to $0.68 per share in the second quarter of 2025, and the current dividend yield is 1.53%. Share repurchases were small at -$0.1B in FY25. One watch item: an executive order could limit distributions and share repurchases during periods of defense-contractor underperformance, which management flags as a potential constraint on capital return.
management.governance: Governance rests on the DEF 14A proxy statement dated March 9, 2026. Under RTX's Director Independence Policy and NYSE listing standards, a majority of directors must be independent; the Board determined that, other than Mr. Calio as a current RTX employee, every nominee for the 2026 Annual Meeting is independent and has no material relationship or transaction interest with RTX. Directors complete an annual questionnaire on relationships and transactions bearing on independence, including the heightened standards for Audit and Human Capital & Compensation Committee members. Related-person transactions above $120,000 in which a director, executive officer, or 5% owner has a material interest require Governance Committee review and approval. The MD&A adds that the Russian government has imposed counter-sanctions targeting certain members of RTX's management team and Board of Directors.

idiosyncratic: Pratt & Whitney Powder Metal Matter: in 2023 Pratt & Whitney determined that a rare condition in powder metal used in certain engine parts requires accelerated inspection of the PW1100 GTF fleet that powers A320neo aircraft, an overhang on cost and cash.

Fixed-price contract exposure: under firm-fixed-price and fixed-price-incentive contracts RTX carries the burden of cost overruns, and inflation, tariffs, and supply-chain constraints can produce losses it cannot always offset through pricing.

Tariffs: RTX has paid approximately $0.5 billion of IEEPA tariffs since inception; refunds ordered by the CIT are subject to the U.S. government's June 2026 appeal, and new tariff regimes may apply to imported products.

Capital-return limits: an executive order may limit distributions, share repurchases, and executive-compensation incentives during periods of defense-contractor underperformance, which the company warns could adversely affect the share price.
Program execution: contract terminations for convenience or default, performance delays, and cost overruns on advanced programs could impair results and future award opportunities.
risks.systemic: Systemic risk centers on U.S. government defense spending and the macro environment. U.S. government sales are a significant portion of consolidated sales, and changes in defense budgets, appropriations, continuing resolutions, or shutdowns could delay awards and payments. The MD&A cites inflation, higher interest rates, foreign-currency movements, and volatile global trade policy as pressures on cost and demand. A global supply chain remains constrained, and management expects disruptions to continue, affecting raw materials, rare earth elements, and microelectronics. Commercial aerospace demand is tied to revenue passenger miles, airline financial health, and airframer performance, so a downturn in air travel would pressure the commercial businesses. These factors are largely outside the company's control and set the backdrop for the scenario weights.

body: We rate RTX BUY with a target range of $205 to $255 against the $193.12 price. The call rests on backlog conversion: a $289B backlog up 22% year over year, a raised full-year adjusted EPS guide of $7.10-$7.25, and wider segment margins in Q2'26. Our Base case of $218 sits below the $234.41 consensus target, so the thesis does not require the multiple to expand from 34.0x trailing or 26.7x forward earnings.

The risks are real and priced into the Bear case of $160, about 17% below the current price: the Powder Metal Matter, tariff and supply-chain cost pressure, and a policy risk to capital return. With a probability-weighted fair value near $216, expected upside of roughly 12%, and reward/risk near 0.7, the risk-reward supports a BUY that depends on execution rather than a re-rating. We would revisit the call if backlog conversion slows or if margins give back the recent gains.
